title: Glenn Close Finally Gets Her Oscar as the Governors Awards Honor Cinema's Greats Tonight
excerpt: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Disney legend Floyd Norman receive honorary Oscars tonight at the 17th Governors Awards in Hollywood — and two indie producers make history.
content:
Tonight in Hollywood, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences hands out the Oscars it owes. Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Disney animation legend Floyd Norman will receive Academy Honorary Awards at the 17th Governors Awards, and independent film producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. The ceremony takes place Sunday evening, November 15, at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, with a reception at 4:30 p.m. PT and dinner and the ceremony at 6 p.m. PT.

For Close, the night ends one of the longest waits in Hollywood history.

Glenn Close: eight nominations, zero wins — until tonight

Close, 79, has been nominated for an Academy Award eight times and has never won. Her first nomination came for The World According to Garp in 1982, and the nods kept coming across five decades — for Fatal Attraction, Dangerous Liaisons, Albert Nobbs, The Wife and Hillbilly Elegy — along the way to a career that also made her unforgettable as Cruella de Vil in 101 Dalmatians and as Norma Desmond in Sunset Boulevard on stage. Long considered among the greatest actors never to win a competitive Oscar, she will be in the room tonight to hold one at last and to give the acceptance speech she has waited decades to make.

Ridley Scott: the blockbuster auteur, honored from afar

Scott, 88, has blended popular success and prestige like few directors ever have — Alien, Blade Runner, Thelma & Louise, Gladiator and Black Hawk Down — but he has never won an Oscar despite four nominations, including best director nods for Thelma & Louise and Black Hawk Down. He will not attend the ceremony in person and will accept the honor in a recorded video.

Floyd Norman: Disney's first Black animator

Norman began his 65-year career at Walt Disney Animation Studios in 1956, becoming the studio's first Black animator. His pencil touched some of the most enduring films in the Disney canon, including Sleeping Beauty, The Jungle Book, Toy Story 2 and Monsters, Inc., and he was named a Disney Legend in 2007. He is only the fourth animator in history to receive an honorary Oscar, joining Walter Lantz, Chuck Jones and Hayao Miyazaki.

Vachon and Koffler make Thalberg history

Vachon and Koffler, co-founders of the New York independent production company Killer Films in 1995, are the first female producing team — and the first independent producers — ever to receive the Thalberg Award, presented to “a creative producer whose body of work reflects a consistently high quality of motion picture production.” In 30 years they have produced more than 100 films, including Boys Don't Cry, Safe, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, Far from Heaven, Carol and Past Lives, for which they earned their first best picture nomination in 2024. Their next project, De Noche, stars Pedro Pascal and Danny Ramirez.

What the Governors Awards are

The Governors Awards are not the Oscars telecast. Named for the Academy's Board of Governors, which selects the recipients, the evening honors lifetime distinction and exceptional contributions to filmmaking — often going to artists with extraordinary careers but no competitive Oscar. The event is presented in partnership with Rolex and produced this year for the first time by Jennifer Todd, a former Academy Producers Branch governor. Recent honorary recipients include Tom Cruise, Debbie Allen, Quincy Jones, Mel Brooks, Angela Bassett, Diane Warren, Peter Weir and Samuel L. Jackson.

What it means

Analysis: tonight is the Academy correcting its own record in public. Close and Scott are two of the most nominated artists never to win, Norman spent 65 years shaping animation while the Academy rarely honored animators at all, and Vachon and Koffler built an independent-film catalog the studios would not touch — and the Thalberg, an award long associated with major-studio moguls, is going to independents for the first time. The Governors Awards do not rewrite the competitive record, but they are the Academy saying, on the record, whose work mattered. For film fans in Laredo and the 956, it is a night when five careers that shaped what we watch finally get the room's full attention.
